message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"3.21","text":"This very man, who alone was a true prophet, appropriately assigned names to each living creature according to the worth of its nature, just as the one who made him did. For whatever he named, that was also the name given by the maker to what had come into being. Why, then, did he still need to partake of a plant so that he might know just what good or evil is? “He was commanded.” But the undiscerning believe these things, supposing that an irrational beast had become more beneficent than God, who created both them and everything.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"κατ᾿ ἀξίαν τῆς φύσεως","chosen":"according to the worth of its nature","rationale":"Preserves ἀξία as worth or corresponding value; “according to what was fitting for its nature” is a smoother possible rendering."},{"source_quote":"καθὼς ὁ πεποιηκὼς αὐτόν","chosen":"just as the one who made him did","rationale":"The masculine αὐτόν refers to the man, not to the neuter ζῷον. The comparison leaves its predicate implicit: it most naturally compares the man’s naming with the maker’s action, though it could compare the appropriateness of the naming with how the maker formed him."},{"source_quote":"εἴ τι γὰρ ἐπωνόμασεν","chosen":"For whatever he named","rationale":"The conditional wording literally permits “if he named anything,” but in context it functions as a general statement about every name he assigned."},{"source_quote":"φυτοῦ χρείαν εἶχε προσλαβεῖν","chosen":"did he still need to partake of a plant","rationale":"The partitive genitive φυτοῦ is retained without inserting an unattested fruit; προσλαβεῖν may denote taking or partaking."},{"source_quote":"„ἐνετέλλετο“","chosen":"“He was commanded.”","rationale":"Reads the middle-passive form passively, as an abrupt reply concerning the man. Since ἐντέλλομαι commonly functions as a deponent meaning “command,” the alternative “[the maker] was commanding” or “he commanded” remains grammatically possible."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"3.22","text":"Nevertheless, a female nature was jointly created as a mate for this man, falling far short of him, as participation falls short of essence, the moon of the sun, and fire of light. She, ruling as a female over the present world, which resembles her, is believed to be the first prophetess, professing prophecy together with all those “among those born of women.” But the other, being male as “Son of Man,” also prophesies the superior things for the coming age as a male age.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ὡς οὐσίας μετουσία","chosen":"as participation falls short of essence","rationale":"Carries forward the idea of falling short from ἀποδέουσα. The compact phrase literally juxtaposes participation and essence."},{"source_quote":"τοῦ νῦν κόσμου ὡς θήλεια ὁμοίου ἄρχουσα","chosen":"ruling as a female over the present world, which resembles her","rationale":"Takes ὁμοίου with κόσμου and understands her as the contextually supplied standard of likeness. “Ruling as a female over the corresponding present world” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"προφητείαν ἐπαγγελλομένη","chosen":"professing prophecy","rationale":"Here ἐπαγγέλλομαι can describe professing or laying claim to prophecy; “promising prophecy” remains possible."},{"source_quote":"τὰ διαφέροντα","chosen":"the superior things","rationale":"διαφέροντα can denote things that excel, fitting the contrast between the present and coming ages. It can alternatively mean “the things that differ.”"},{"source_quote":"καὶ τὰ διαφέροντα ὡς ἄρσενι τῷ μέλλοντι αἰῶνι προφητεύει","chosen":"also prophesies the superior things for the coming age as a male age","rationale":"The dative ἄρσενι agrees with τῷ μέλλοντι αἰῶνι, characterizing the coming age as male in contrast with the female present world; it does not merely state what befits the male prophet."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἀποδέουσα -αὐτοῦ","issue":"The selected print places an anomalous hyphen immediately before αὐτοῦ. The translation provisionally treats it as nonlexical punctuation and takes αὐτοῦ as the genitive complement of ἀποδέουσα.","proposed_reading":"ἀποδέουσα αὐτοῦ","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ὡς ἡλίου σελήνη; ὡς φωτὸς τὸ πῦρ","issue":"The selected print has a Greek question mark between two parallel comparisons. It may be deliberate editorial punctuation, but it interrupts the continuing comparative construction; the translation provisionally punctuates the sequence continuously.","proposed_reading":"ὡς ἡλίου σελήνη, ὡς φωτὸς τὸ πῦρ","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"3.23","text":"Let there be, then, two generic prophecies for us: the masculine one (and let it be specified that the first, being male, has thereafter been placed second according to the principle of progression, whereas the second, being female, was appointed to come first in the procession of the pairs)—the one, then, who is “among those born of women,” professing prophecy as the female belonging to the present world, wants to be believed to be masculine. Therefore, stealing the male’s seeds and attending to them with her own seeds of the flesh, she brings forth the offspring together as though they were all her own—that is, the words. And she promises to give present earthly wealth as a dowry, wishing to exchange the slow for the quick, the brief for the greater.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"δύο οὖν ἡμῖν γενικαὶ ἔστωσαν προφητεῖαι","chosen":"Let there be, then, two generic prophecies for us","rationale":"γενικαί describes prophecies belonging to broad kinds or classes; “universal prophecies” is another possible rendering."},{"source_quote":"κατὰ τὸν τῆς προόδου λόγον","chosen":"according to the principle of progression","rationale":"λόγος denotes the governing principle or rationale, while πρόοδος describes progression or procession."},{"source_quote":"ἐν τῇ τῶν συζυγιῶν προελεύσει","chosen":"in the procession of the pairs","rationale":"συζυγίαι are paired counterparts, while προέλευσις can denote their procession or ordered sequence."},{"source_quote":"τοῖς ἰδίοις τῆς σαρκὸς σπέρμασιν ἐπισκέπτουσα","chosen":"attending to them with her own seeds of the flesh","rationale":"Retains the exact printed participle ἐπισκέπτουσα, from ἐπισκέπτομαι, which can mean inspecting, visiting, or attending to something; the stolen male seeds are understood as its implicit object. “Inspecting them with her own seeds” is lexically possible but less natural in context. The earlier rendering “covering them” would correspond more directly to a different form, ἐπισκέπουσα, which is not the supplied reading and is not adopted as a correction."},{"source_quote":"ὡς ὅλα ἴδια συνεκφέρει τὰ γεννήματα","chosen":"she brings forth the offspring together as though they were all her own","rationale":"Preserves both the claim that all the offspring are represented as hers and the συν- force of συνεκφέρει, which links what comes from the two sets of seeds."},{"source_quote":"τῷ ταχεῖ τὸ βραδύ, τὸ βραχὺ τῷ μείζονι ὑπαλλάξαι","chosen":"to exchange the slow for the quick, the brief for the greater","rationale":"Treats the accusatives as what is exchanged for the dative counterparts. The direction of exchange can be construed in reverse with ὑπαλλάσσω."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"3.24","text":"Yet she not only dares to speak and hear of many gods, but also gives assurance that she herself will become one; and in the hope of becoming what she does not possess by nature, she also destroys what she does possess. And as a female, when she comes into her menstrual periods, she is stained with blood under the pretext of sacrifices and so defiles those who touch her. And whenever, after conceiving, she gives birth to temporary kings who shed much blood, she stirs up wars. As for those who long to learn truth from her, by saying everything in contradictory ways and providing many and various services, she makes them keep seeking and find nothing until death itself. For from the beginning she has lain before blind people as an occasion of death; by prophesying deceptive, ambiguous, and crooked things, she deceives those who believe.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτὴ γενέσθαι πιστοῦσα","chosen":"but also gives assurance that she herself will become one","rationale":"The active participle from πιστόω has the force of making certain, confirming, or assuring. “Confidently claiming that she herself will become one” is a viable contextual alternative, but ordinary “believing” would obscure this causative or confirmatory force."},{"source_quote":"ἐλπίδι τοῦ γενέσθαι ὃ μὴ ἔχει φύσιν καὶ ὃ ἔχει προσαπολλύουσα","chosen":"in the hope of becoming what she does not possess by nature, she also destroys what she does possess","rationale":"The parallel ὃ μὴ ἔχει and ὃ ἔχει supports taking her as the implicit subject of both and understanding φύσιν as an accusative of respect, “by nature.” Material alternatives are “in the hope of becoming what she lacks the nature or capacity to become, she also destroys what she possesses” and the impersonal “becoming what has no nature and destroying what does.”"},{"source_quote":"ἐν ἐμμηνίοις γινομένη","chosen":"when she comes into her menstrual periods","rationale":"ἐμμήνια denotes menstruation or menstrual discharge; the rendering retains the author’s female-body imagery."},{"source_quote":"τοὺς προσκαίρους τίκτῃ βασιλεῖς, τοὺς αἷμα πολὺ χέοντας ἐγείρει πολέμους","chosen":"she gives birth to temporary kings who shed much blood, she stirs up wars","rationale":"Takes τοὺς αἷμα πολὺ χέοντας as an appositional description of the kings, which provides the more natural agents for shedding blood. Because the participle can also agree with πολέμους, the alternative is “she stirs up wars that shed much blood.”"},{"source_quote":"πολλὰς καὶ διαφόρους παρέχειν ὑπουργίας","chosen":"providing many and various services","rationale":"ὑπουργία denotes service or assistance. If these are demands placed upon the seekers rather than services offered to them, “many and varied tasks of service” is possible."},{"source_quote":"θανάτου κεῖται πρόφασις","chosen":"has lain ... as an occasion of death","rationale":"πρόφασις can mean pretext, occasion, ostensible cause, or alleged reason. “Pretext for death” is more formally literal, while “occasion of death” better expresses the resulting harm in context."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"3.25","text":"Therefore she imposed an equivocal name on her firstborn, calling him Cain, which admits a twofold interpretation; for it is interpreted both as “possession” and as “jealousy,” since in what was to come he was destined to be jealous of either a wife or possessions or the parents’ affection toward him. But if none of these things actually came about, even so, calling him “possession” has hit the mark well; for she acquired him first, and this also proved useful to her. For he was a “murderer,” “and a liar,” and, amid sins, was unwilling to live quietly even while ruling. Moreover, those who came from his line became the first adulterers; they fashioned psalteries and lyres and became bronzesmiths of weapons of war. Therefore, how the prophecy of the descendants too, full of adulterers and psalteries, secretly stirs up wars through sensual pleasures!","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀμφοτερίζον ἐπέθηκεν ὄνομα","chosen":"she imposed an equivocal name","rationale":"ἀμφοτερίζον describes a name that goes in both directions or bears two senses, as the following clause explains."},{"source_quote":"ὃ διχῇ ἔχει τῆς ἑρμηνείας τὴν ἐκδοχήν","chosen":"which admits a twofold interpretation","rationale":"The expression describes two possible outcomes or explanations of the name’s interpretation."},{"source_quote":"ὡς ζηλοῦν αὐτοῦ μέλλοντος ἐν τοῖς ἐσομένοις ἢ γυναῖκα ἢ κτήματα ἢ τὴν τῶν γονέων πρὸς αὐτὸν στοργήν","chosen":"since in what was to come he was destined to be jealous of either a wife or possessions or the parents’ affection toward him","rationale":"αὐτοῦ is the genitive subject of μέλλοντος, with ζηλοῦν as its complementary infinitive; it does not supply a separate target of jealousy. The later αὐτόν in πρὸς αὐτόν may refer to Cain or to another contextually implied male, so “toward him” preserves that referential uncertainty."},{"source_quote":"τὸ „κτῆμα“ λέγεσθαι καλῶς ἐπιτέτευκται","chosen":"calling him “possession” has hit the mark well","rationale":"ἐπιτυγχάνω conveys attaining or hitting the mark; the infinitive phrase functions as the subject."},{"source_quote":"„φονεὺς“ γὰρ ἦν „καὶ ψεύστης“","chosen":"For he was a “murderer,” “and a liar,”","rationale":"Keeps καὶ within the second quoted expression, following the source’s quotation boundaries rather than placing “and” outside the quotation."},{"source_quote":"μετὰ ἁμαρτιῶν ἡσυχάζειν μηδὲ ἐπὶ τῷ ἄρχειν θέλων","chosen":"amid sins, was unwilling to live quietly even while ruling","rationale":"Takes μετά as accompaniment or surrounding circumstance and ἐπὶ τῷ ἄρχειν temporally. Alternatives include “unwilling to rest with his sins, even in ruling” or taking the final phrase as “even for the sake of ruling.”"},{"source_quote":"ψαλτήρια καὶ κιθάρας ἡρμόσαντο","chosen":"they fashioned psalteries and lyres","rationale":"ἁρμόζω can mean fitting together, constructing, or tuning. “Fashioned” fits the account of originating instruments while “tuned” remains possible."},{"source_quote":"χαλκεῖς ὅπλων πολεμικῶν ἐγένοντο","chosen":"became bronzesmiths of weapons of war","rationale":"χαλκεῖς specifically denotes workers in copper or bronze and, more broadly, metalworkers; the genitive identifies their products as weapons used in war."},{"source_quote":"λανθανόντως διὰ τῶν ἡδυπαθειῶν ὡς τοὺς πολέμους ἐγείρει","chosen":"how ... secretly stirs up wars through sensual pleasures!","rationale":"Takes ὡς before the finite clause as exclamatory, “how,” while λανθανόντως indicates that the effect operates unnoticed or secretly. A declarative reading such as “that it secretly stirs up wars” is possible, but a standalone hedge such as “as it were” is not required by the construction."}],"source_issues":[]}]}
